# The Underlines of Strangers

The book cost fifty cents. It lay on a folding table in a church basement, third row from the radiator, spine bleached and creased into a soft white valley, its pages gone the color of weak tea. A Signet paperback of *Middlemarch*, printed sometime in the seventies, cover price $1.95 — a price that seems to belong to another civilization. Outside it was raining in the way October rains, that patient sideways drizzle, and the basement smelled of coffee, damp wool, and the particular sweetness of old paper, which is really the smell of lignin slowly surrendering. I wasn't looking for *Middlemarch*. I had read it years ago, in college, in a hurry, the way you read assigned things. But the book looked like it had been loved, and loved books at fifty cents are the best bargain in the world, so I bought it.

I opened it on the bus home. Inside the front cover, in blue ballpoint, in a careful cursive: *To Ruth — for the long winter ahead. All my love, Harold. Dec. 1974.* And beneath that, in different ink from a different decade, a second line: *Ruth Halloway, March 1991.*

I have thought about that second signature more than is strictly reasonable. Why would a woman sign her own name in a book she had owned for seventeen years? Booksellers will tell you they see this constantly — people re-inscribing themselves into their own possessions. After a divorce, maybe. After a move, a widowhood, a diagnosis. Some moment when the self needed restating, and the nearest available document happened to be the flyleaf of a novel about a woman trying to give her life away to something larger than herself.

A used book is an archaeological site, and the dig is always a surprise. Across years of haunting library sales and thrift-shop shelves I have found, serving as bookmarks: a hardware store receipt itemized down to washers; a boarding pass to Denver; a photograph of two teenagers squinting in beach light; pressed violets gone tissue-thin; a toothpick wrapper folded into a tiny accordion, for reasons no one will ever recover. Once, in a gardening manual, a laminated memorial card — a man's face, gentle, and the dates 1941–2016. He was holding place at the chapter on pruning roses. Whether he was the reader or merely the occasion for the book's purchase, there is no way to know. The ambiguity isn't a flaw. It's the whole point.

The pencil in my *Middlemarch* belongs, I decided, to Ruth. Soft lead, confident strokes. She underlined heavily through the early chapters, where Dorothea burns with the desire to give herself to something vast, and the marks track that hunger nearly sentence by sentence. Then they thin. By the middle of the book they stop altogether, somewhere in the long wilderness of the Casaubon marriage, and never resume. Every abandoned book preserves the exact coordinates of an interruption. *She stopped here,* it says. *Here is where I put you down.* Did she die? Get bored? Did life simply elbow its way in — a job, a grandchild, a bad knee, a winter worse than the one Harold had promised the book against? There is no answer. There is only the page where the graphite ends, and the strange obligation a stranger's silence can place upon you.

Consider the abandoned bookmark as a genre of writing. Memoirs lie, diaries curate, letters perform — but nobody curates their placeholder. Nobody chooses, for posterity, the prescription dated a week before everything changed, or the ticket stub for a train to the city they moved away from. These objects were never meant to be seen; that's what makes them true. A bookmark is a timestamp made of paper, and when the reading stops forever, the book becomes a clock. It keeps, for decades, the hour of somebody's interruption. Museums preserve swords and crowns and try, mostly in vain, to convey what it was like to be alive. A used paperback does it with a bus transfer and a smudge of pencil.

Which is why digital reading troubles me in a way I can't quite argue myself out of. The e-reader is wonderful — I mean that sincerely, the adjustable type alone justifies its existence — but it is hygienic in a way that borders on sterilization. Your highlights exist, technically, but they live on a server, formatted identically to everyone else's, retrievable only if you remember to look. Amazon will even show you the "Popular Highlights": this sentence was highlighted by 3,204 readers, it announces, converting private response into consensus, idiosyncrasy into statistics. And when a reader dies, their account is closed with tidy finality. The device is wiped, resold, recycled. Nothing remains to be found on a folding table by a stranger in a church basement.

Paper fails by decay, which takes decades and leaves ruins. Digital fails by deletion, which is instant and total. The cloud does not yellow. It does not crack along the spine. It cannot hold a pressed violet flat for forty years. Whatever we are building on those servers, it is not a sediment; it is a surface, endlessly refreshed, on which nothing accumulates.

And accumulation matters, because a shelf of marked-up books turns out to be an autobiography written by accident. Open any of my paperbacks and I can tell you roughly who I was when I marked it — not from the date I sometimes scrawl on the back cover, but from *what* I underlined. My twenty-three-year-old self bracketed passages about ambition and underlined passages about solitude, and did so earnestly, with a heavy hand. Meeting him in the margins is humbling. Sometimes he is smarter than I remembered being; more often he is performing seriousness, underlining the impressive sentence instead of the true one. Either way, the correspondence continues: I leave notes for the next self, knowing he'll find them, not knowing when. Rereading is how the living talk to themselves across time. Marginalia is the postal service.

We forget that this is ancient behavior. The medieval scribes — anonymous, cloistered, copying sacred texts by candlelight — survived the centuries not through their devotions but through their complaints, scribbled in margins and colophons. The vellum was hairy. The scriptorium was freezing. Their hands ached; their eyes stung; the wine was bad. One exhausted copyist, reaching the end of his labor, begged posterity for exactly one reward: *here ends the whole work; for Christ's sake, give me a drink.* There's something perfect in this. The texts they copied are enshrined and revered, and the humans survive only as grumbles in the white space — which means the white space, the part everyone skips, is where the people are.

Margins have toppled certainties before. In 1637, Pierre de Fermat, doodling in the margin of Diophantus's *Arithmetica*, noted that he had discovered a truly marvelous proof of a certain proposition, which the margin was unfortunately too narrow to contain. He never wrote it down elsewhere, so far as anyone knows. Mathematicians tormented themselves for three and a half centuries until Andrew Wiles finally proved the theorem in the 1990s — by methods Fermat could not conceivably have possessed, which raises the delightful possibility that the greatest mathematician of his age was simply wrong in a margin. The most consequential piece of marginalia ever written was, quite possibly, a bluff. Either way: the margins are where certainty goes to be tested.

Samuel Taylor Coleridge is the patron saint of all this. He wrote so prolifically in the margins of other people's books that friends began lending him volumes expressly hoping he would deface them — the annotation was the gift. He all but gave the practice its English name, *marginalia*, and elevated it into a minor art form; his penciled remarks were sometimes worth more than the books they adorned. And when William Blake read Joshua Reynolds's *Discourses on Art*, he didn't merely disagree — he conducted open warfare in the white space, at one point declaring that Reynolds was hired to depress art. The margins became a courtroom where a dead authority stood perpetual trial before a living reader. Every furious "NO!" in a used book is Blake's descendant.

Modern scholarship agrees. When a major writer dies, archivists descend on their personal libraries with gloves and reverence, because the annotations are often the most intimate manuscript left behind. Researchers have spent years reconstructing David Foster Wallace's mind from the pencils in the margins of his books, now housed in Texas. You can learn what a person argued with, what they envied, what they couldn't stop noticing. The published work is the performance. The marginalia is the rehearsal.

Because that is what an underline fundamentally is: attention made visible. Reading is invisible — it leaves no sound, no product, no trace — and so much of interior life goes unwitnessed, even by the people closest to us. But a pencil stroke is the physical residue of a consciousness moving through a sentence. To read a marked-up book is therefore to read twice: once alone, and once in step with a stranger whose taste you infer stroke by stroke, whose patience you can measure by where the marks stop. You know exactly which clause snagged her eye. Most spouses don't know that about each other. And it changes your own reading — you argue with her, defend the passages she skipped, feel personally betrayed when she skims the best chapter. You are having a relationship with someone you will never meet, mediated by graphite and dead trees.

I understand the objection. Some readers want virgin pages; a stranger's pencil feels like graffiti, a contamination of the one space they thought was theirs. Reading is intimate, and they want it unmediated. Fair enough — but the purity is a fantasy anyway. No book arrives unmarked: reviews tell us what to admire, syllabi tell us what to test, the whole ambient culture pre-underlines everything before we touch it. At least an honest pencil admits what it's doing. A used book doesn't pretend the reading was yours alone. It shows you the crowd you were always reading with.

Even libraries knew this once. Find an old discard with its borrowing card still glued in the back — the little pocket, the stamped dates — and you'll find a relay race of attention. 1963. 1968. 1974. 1983. Different hands, different lives, none of whom met, all of them momentarily joined by a single object passed hand to hand like a bucket in a fire line. The due-date card was the original social network, and unlike ours, it required proximity and trust. Now the same connections exist as anonymized rows in a database, invisible even to the people they describe. Progress, presumably. Though nothing in a database will ever fall out of a book onto a stranger's floor and make them wonder about a woman named Ruth.

I wasn't always a convert. For years I treated books as objects of worship: spines uncracked, covers unbent, dust jackets preserved like museum glass. I broke in new paperbacks carefully, flexing the binding the way you gentle a horse. It took me an embarrassingly long time to notice that my most pristine books were frequently my least-read ones — that reverence had become a substitute for attention. What finally tipped me was the realization that I wanted my life legible inside my objects. I wanted evidence. Now I write in everything, and when I finish a book I date the back cover, a small private ritual, a stamp in a passport. The first tentative pencil marks felt like vandalism. Within a year they felt necessary. Now a clean page makes me itch.

So here is what happens to my fifty-cent *Middlemarch*. I will read it again — properly this time — but in tandem with Ruth, following her pencil like a guide through familiar country. I'll notice what she noticed, and I'll notice where she noticed it, because *where* matters: she underlined hardest in the chapters about wanting your life to mean something, which suggests that in the winter of 1974, that question was not abstract for her. I'll read slowly through the middle of the book, past the place where her marks end, carrying the reading forward on her behalf — someone has to finish this, I'll think, might as well be me. And when I reach the last page, I'll take a pen and add my line beneath hers on the flyleaf: name, date. Not ownership. Membership. A chain letter written in pencil, each link a stranger agreeing to keep faith with the last.

George Eliot ended *Middlemarch* by insisting that the world's goodness grows partly out of "unhistoric acts" — the small, unmonumented deeds of people who lived faithfully hidden lives and rest in unvisited tombs, their influence "incalculably diffusive" through everyone around them. It is one of the great endings in literature precisely because it relocates significance from the famous to the unnoticed. Marginalia is the smallest of unhistoric acts. No plaque, no credit, just graphite in the quiet of an evening — and yet it propagates. From Harold to Ruth, from Ruth to me, from me to whoever buys this copy off some future folding table when my own shelves are scattered, as all shelves eventually are. That person will open the cover, find three names in two kinds of ink and two kinds of pencil, and feel — for a moment, the way I did on the bus — less alone among the dead. Fifty cents for that. It is the best bargain in the world.
